claim: Adult stem cells are maintained in niches, specialized microenvironments that regulate their self-renewal and differentiation.
source: Adult stem cells are maintained in niches, specialized microenvironments that regulate their self-renewal and differentiation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about stem cell biology, supported by the citation (Drummond-Barbosa, 2019; Greenspan et al., 2015) in the following sentence.

claim: In the adult Drosophila testis stem cell niche, somatic hub cells produce signals that regulate adjacent germline stem cells (GSCs) and somatic cyst stem cells (CySCs).
source: In the adult Drosophila testis stem cell niche, somatic hub cells produce signals that regulate adjacent germline stem cells (GSCs) and somatic cyst stem cells (CySCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila testis niche structure and function.

claim: Hub cells are normally quiescent.
source: Hub cells are normally quiescent, but after complete genetic ablation of CySCs, they can proliferate and transdifferentiate into new CySCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hub cell behavior, supported by prior research.

claim: After complete genetic ablation of CySCs, hub cells can proliferate and transdifferentiate into new CySCs.
source: Hub cells are normally quiescent, but after complete genetic ablation of CySCs, they can proliferate and transdifferentiate into new CySCs.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling is upregulated in hub cells after CySC ablation.
source: Here we find that Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling is upregulated in hub cells after CySC ablation and that the ability of testes to recover from ablation is inhibited by reduced EGFR signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ability of testes to recover from CySC ablation is inhibited by reduced EGFR signaling.
source: Here we find that Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling is upregulated in hub cells after CySC ablation and that the ability of testes to recover from ablation is inhibited by reduced EGFR signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and Tables 5-6.

claim: Activation of the EGFR pathway in hub cells is sufficient to induce their proliferation and transdifferentiation into CySCs.
source: In addition, activation of the EGFR pathway in hub cells is sufficient to induce their proliferation and transdifferentiation into CySCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 1-3 and Tables 1-3.

claim: EGFR signaling, which is normally required in adult cyst cells, is actively inhibited in adult hub cells to maintain their fate.
source: We propose that EGFR signaling, which is normally required in adult cyst cells, is actively inhibited in adult hub cells to maintain their fate but is repurposed to drive stem cell regeneration after CySC ablation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and supported by data showing that inhibitors maintain hub cell quiescence.

claim: EGFR signaling is repurposed to drive stem cell regeneration after CySC ablation.
source: We propose that EGFR signaling, which is normally required in adult cyst cells, is actively inhibited in adult hub cells to maintain their fate but is repurposed to drive stem cell regeneration after CySC ablation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental findings showing EGFR upregulation after ablation and its requirement for recovery.

claim: Stem cells can be regenerated even after complete loss of a stem cell population.
source: Loss of a stem cell population due to injury or aging can be detrimental to tissue function, but recent studies have shown that stem cells can be regenerated even after complete loss of a stem cell population (Beumer and Clevers, 2021; Greenspan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: In the Drosophila testis, both germline and somatic stem cells can be regenerated de novo by conversion of other cell types into stem cells.
source: In the Drosophila testis, both germline and somatic stem cells can be regenerated de novo by conversion of other cell types into stem cells, which makes this well-characterized system an exceptional model for studying the dynamics of stem cell regeneration in vivo (Brawley and Matunis, 2004; Cheng et al., 2008; Greenspan and Matunis, 2018; Hétié et al., 2014, Sheng et al., 2009; Voog et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that trigger stem cell regeneration events remain largely unknown.
source: The molecular mechanisms that trigger these events remain largely unknown, but elucidating them could lead to the development of novel regenerative and anti-aging therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The Drosophila testis niche contains a cluster of somatic hub cells that sends signals to two types of stem cells: germline stem cells (GSCs) and somatic cyst stem cells (CySCs).
source: The Drosophila testis niche contains a cluster of somatic hub cells that sends signals to two types of stem cells: germline stem cells (GSCs), which give rise to sperm, and somatic cyst stem cells (CySCs), which give rise to the cyst cells that encase differentiating germ cells (Figure 1A; Hardy et al., 1979).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: GSCs give rise to sperm.
source: germline stem cells (GSCs), which give rise to sperm
evidence: This is established knowledge about GSC function.

claim: CySCs give rise to the cyst cells that encase differentiating germ cells.
source: somatic cyst stem cells (CySCs), which give rise to the cyst cells that encase differentiating germ cells (Figure 1A; Hardy et al., 1979).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: CySCs and hub cells derive from a common pool of precursor cells and are specified early in embryogenesis.
source: CySCs and hub cells derive from a common pool of precursor cells and are specified early in embryogenesis (Dinardo et al., 2011; Le Bras and Van Doren, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hub cells are completely quiescent in adult flies.
source: Hub cells are completely quiescent in adult flies, but after injury to the testis, in the form of genetic ablation of CySCs, they can exit quiescence, leave the hub, and transdifferentiate into CySCs, thereby replenishing the lost population of stem cells (Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: After injury to the testis in the form of genetic ablation of CySCs, hub cells can exit quiescence, leave the hub, and transdifferentiate into CySCs, thereby replenishing the lost population of stem cells.
source: Hub cells are completely quiescent in adult flies, but after injury to the testis, in the form of genetic ablation of CySCs, they can exit quiescence, leave the hub, and transdifferentiate into CySCs, thereby replenishing the lost population of stem cells (Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The molecular signals that trigger hub cells to re-enter the cell cycle are not known.
source: The molecular signals that trigger hub cells to re-enter the cell cycle are not known but are likely acting upstream of Cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (Cdk4) and its binding partner Cyclin D, since the forced over-expression of these two proteins is sufficient to drive hub cells out of quiescence and into the transdifferentiation program (Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The molecular signals that trigger hub cells to re-enter the cell cycle are likely acting upstream of Cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (Cdk4) and its binding partner Cyclin D.
source: The molecular signals that trigger hub cells to re-enter the cell cycle are not known but are likely acting upstream of Cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (Cdk4) and its binding partner Cyclin D, since the forced over-expression of these two proteins is sufficient to drive hub cells out of quiescence and into the transdifferentiation program (Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research showing that Cdk4 and Cyclin D overexpression drives hub cell transdifferentiation.

claim: Forced over-expression of Cdk4 and Cyclin D is sufficient to drive hub cells out of quiescence and into the transdifferentiation program.
source: the forced over-expression of these two proteins is sufficient to drive hub cells out of quiescence and into the transdifferentiation program (Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Conversion of adult hub cells into CySCs occurs when the Snail-family transcription factor Escargot is knocked down directly in hub cells.
source: Similarly, conversion of adult hub cells into CySCs also occurs when the Snail-family transcription factor Escargot or the tumor suppressor and Cdk4/Cyclin D target Retinoblastoma-family protein (Rbf) is knocked down directly in hub cells (Greenspan and Matunis, 2018; Voog et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Conversion of adult hub cells into CySCs occurs when the tumor suppressor and Cdk4/Cyclin D target Retinoblastoma-family protein (Rbf) is knocked down directly in hub cells.
source: Similarly, conversion of adult hub cells into CySCs also occurs when the Snail-family transcription factor Escargot or the tumor suppressor and Cdk4/Cyclin D target Retinoblastoma-family protein (Rbf) is knocked down directly in hub cells (Greenspan and Matunis, 2018; Voog et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are relatively few examples of transdifferentiation in vivo.
source: Although many examples of transdifferentiation have been reported in vitro, there are relatively few examples in vivo (Merrell and Stanger, 2016), making the upstream events that instruct hub cells to transdifferentiate upon injury to the Drosophila testis of interest.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The EGFR/MAPK signaling pathway is a conserved receptor tyrosine kinase pathway that regulates many aspects of development including cell survival, growth, proliferation, and differentiation.
source: The epidermal growth factor receptor/mitogen-activated protein kinase (EGFR/MAPK) signaling pathway is a conserved receptor tyrosine kinase pathway that regulates many aspects of development including cell survival, growth, proliferation, and differentiation (Wee and Wang, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the developing Drosophila testis, the EGFR signaling pathway is essential for the formation and function of cyst cells.
source: In the developing Drosophila testis, the EGFR signaling pathway is essential for the formation and function of cyst cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge that will be supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Notch is expressed in all somatic gonadal precursor cells (SGPs) and required for hub cell fate during embryogenesis.
source: While Notch is expressed in all somatic gonadal precursor cells (SGPs) and required for hub cell fate during embryogenesis, EGFR signaling is only expressed in a subset, repressing hub cell fate and enabling these cells to differentiate into cyst lineage cells (Kitadate and Kobayashi, 2010; Okegbe and DiNardo, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EGFR signaling is only expressed in a subset of SGPs, repressing hub cell fate and enabling these cells to differentiate into cyst lineage cells.
source: While Notch is expressed in all somatic gonadal precursor cells (SGPs) and required for hub cell fate during embryogenesis, EGFR signaling is only expressed in a subset, repressing hub cell fate and enabling these cells to differentiate into cyst lineage cells (Kitadate and Kobayashi, 2010; Okegbe and DiNardo, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In adult testes, EGFR signaling is required in cyst lineage cells for their encapsulation of germ cells.
source: In adult testes, EGFR signaling is required in cyst lineage cells for their encapsulation of germ cells, and this association is vital for germ cell differentiation and maturation into sperm (Hudson et al., 2013; Kiger et al., 2000; Sarkar et al., 2007; Schulz et al., 2002; Tran et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The association between cyst lineage cells and germ cells is vital for germ cell differentiation and maturation into sperm.
source: In adult testes, EGFR signaling is required in cyst lineage cells for their encapsulation of germ cells, and this association is vital for germ cell differentiation and maturation into sperm (Hudson et al., 2013; Kiger et al., 2000; Sarkar et al., 2007; Schulz et al., 2002; Tran et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: EGFR signaling is required in the adult germline stem cells to regulate the frequency of their divisions.
source: EGFR signaling is also required in the adult germline stem cells to regulate the frequency of their divisions (Parrott et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Whether EGFR signaling has a role in adult hub cells has not yet been investigated.
source: Whether EGFR signaling has a role in adult hub cells has not yet been investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Over-expression of Pointed (either isoform, P1 or P2) in the hub resulted in significant numbers of testes with PH3-positive hub cells.
source: Over-expression of Pointed (either isoform, P1 or P2; Klaes et al., 1994) or a constitutively active form of EGFR in the hub resulted in significant numbers of testes with PH3-positive hub cells (7% of testes, n = 55, for P1; 6% of testes, n = 100, for P2; or 4% of testes, n = 117, for EGFR; Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Over-expression of a constitutively active form of EGFR in the hub resulted in significant numbers of testes with PH3-positive hub cells.
source: Over-expression of Pointed (either isoform, P1 or P2; Klaes et al., 1994) or a constitutively active form of EGFR in the hub resulted in significant numbers of testes with PH3-positive hub cells (7% of testes, n = 55, for P1; 6% of testes, n = 100, for P2; or 4% of testes, n = 117, for EGFR; Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Over-expression of constitutively active Ras for 3 or 5 days caused significant numbers of testes with PH3-positive hub cells.
source: Over-expression of constitutively active Ras for 7 days caused testes to develop grossly abnormal or missing hubs (data not shown), complicating the scoring process; however, we found significant numbers of testes with PH3-positive hub cells after a shorter period (3 or 5 days) of constitutively active Ras expression in the hub (11% of testes, n = 18, after 3 days, or 6% of testes, n = 36, after 5 days; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: The percentage of testes with PH3-positive hub cells upon over-expression of EGFR/MAPK pathway components is similar to that seen during recovery from CySC ablation.
source: The percentage of testes with PH3-positive hub cells upon over-expression of EGFR/MAPK pathway components (Table 1) is similar to that seen during recovery from CySC ablation (6–10% testes have PH3-positive hub cells at 1–5 days after ablation; Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison between current experimental data and prior research.

claim: Activation of EGFR signaling in the hub is sufficient to drive quiescent hub cells into mitosis.
source: We conclude that activation of EGFR signaling in the hub is sufficient to drive quiescent hub cells into mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from the screen.

claim: Over-expressing activated forms of Heartless or Pvr in hub cells did not result in statistically significant numbers of testes with PH3-positive hub cells compared to the negative control.
source: Although a few testes acquired PH3-positive hub cells after over-expression of activated Heartless or Pvr, these results were not statistically significant compared to the negative control (Table 1), and we found no PH3-positive hub cells after over-expressing activated Breathless or InR.
evidence: This is a negative result from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: No PH3-positive hub cells were found after over-expressing activated Breathless or InR in hub cells.
source: Although a few testes acquired PH3-positive hub cells after over-expression of activated Heartless or Pvr, these results were not statistically significant compared to the negative control (Table 1), and we found no PH3-positive hub cells after over-expressing activated Breathless or InR.
evidence: This is a negative result from experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Activation of EGFR within hub cells plays a unique role in forcing these cells to lose quiescence and re-enter the cell cycle.
source: These results suggest that activation of EGFR within hub cells plays a unique role in forcing these cells to lose quiescence and re-enter the cell cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of EGFR activation compared to other receptor tyrosine kinases.

claim: Adult hub cells in otherwise unperturbed testes do not cell-autonomously require EGFR.
source: We therefore conclude that adult hub cells in otherwise unperturbed testes do not cell-autonomously require EGFR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing no phenotype with EGFR knockdown in hub cells (Table 2).

claim: Notch does not play a role in maintaining hub cell quiescence in the adult testis.
source: These results suggest that Notch does not play a role in maintaining hub cell quiescence in the adult testis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing no phenotype with Notch manipulation in hub cells (Table 2).

claim: Activation of EGFR signaling in adult hub cells is sufficient to cause their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
source: We conclude that activation of EGFR signaling in adult hub cells is sufficient to cause their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on G-TRACE lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2 and Table 3.

claim: Sprouty is required in adult hub cells to maintain their quiescence.
source: After 7 days of knockdown, a significant number of testes had PH3-positive hub cells (3% of testes, n = 144; Table 1; Figure 3A), confirming that Sprouty is required in adult hub cells to maintain their quiescence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Knockdown of Sprouty in adult hub cells is sufficient to cause their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
source: To determine if hub cells depleted for Sprouty can also transdifferentiate into CySCs, we expressed Sprouty RNAi together with G-TRACE in adult hub cells (E132-Gal4, Gal80ts > UAS-sprouty-RNAi + G-TRACE). After 8 days, a significant number of testes had GFP-marked cells outside the hub (Table 3; Figure 3E), indicating that knockdown of Sprouty in adult hub cells is sufficient to cause their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 3.

claim: PTEN is required in adult hub cells to maintain their quiescence.
source: After 7 days of PTEN knockdown in the hub (E132-Gal4, Gal80ts > UAS-Pten-RNAi), a significant number of testes had PH3-positive hub cells (3% of testes, n = 125; Table 1; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: PTEN is required in adult hub cells to prevent their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
source: Knockdown of PTEN in adult hub cells is also sufficient to cause their conversion to cyst lineage cells: after expressing PTEN RNAi together with G-TRACE in adult hub cells for 7 days (E132-Gal4, Gal80ts > UAS-Pten-RNAi + G-TRACE), we found a significant number of testes with GFP-marked cells outside the hub (Table 3; Figure 3F). We conclude that PTEN is required in adult hub cells to maintain their quiescence and prevent their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 3.

claim: PTEN acts in hub cells by inhibiting EGFR rather than by regulating the PI3K pathway.
source: We did not find PH3-positive hub cells after over-expressing or knocking down other members of the canonical PI3K pathway (Table 1; Appendix 1), which supports the idea that PTEN acts in hub cells by inhibiting EGFR rather than by regulating the PI3K pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on negative results with other PI3K pathway components.

claim: The EGFR/MAPK pathway is up-regulated in hub cells upon knockdown of PTEN or Sprouty.
source: After 7 days at restrictive temperature (31 °C), PTEN and Sprouty knockdown flies both had significantly higher levels of dpERK in the hub than control (y w) flies (Figure 3C), confirming that the EGFR/MAPK pathway is up-regulated in hub cells upon knockdown of PTEN or Sprouty.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The EGFR pathway is actively inhibited in adult hub cells by at least two cell-autonomous inhibitors, Sprouty and PTEN, which maintain hub cell quiescence and prevent their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
source: Taken together, these results support the hypothesis that the EGFR pathway is actively inhibited in adult hub cells by at least two cell-autonomous inhibitors, Sprouty and PTEN, which maintain hub cell quiescence and prevent their conversion to cyst lineage cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: Argos is required non-cell-autonomously to maintain hub cell quiescence in adult testes.
source: To test this hypothesis, we drove expression of UAS-argos-RNAi conditionally in adult testes using the cyst lineage driver C587-Gal4, Gal80ts (C587-Gal4, Gal80ts > UAS-argos-RNAi). After 7 days of knockdown, we found a significant number of testes with PH3-positive hub cells (2% of testes, n = 287; Table 1; Figure 3D), supporting the hypothesis that Argos is required non-cell-autonomously to maintain hub cell quiescence in adult testes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Over-expression of EGF ligands is not sufficient to trigger loss of hub cell quiescence.
source: We conclude that over-expression of EGF ligands is not sufficient to trigger loss of hub cell quiescence, or to enhance the loss of quiescence caused by knockdown of the Spitz antagonist Argos, but the reason for these results is not clear.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on negative experimental results shown in Table 4.

claim: EGFR pathway activity is up-regulated in hub cells after CySC ablation.
source: By contrast, in experimental testes, the levels of dpERK staining in the hub were significantly higher than in control testes (Figure 4B–C), suggesting that the EGFR pathway activity is up-regulated in hub cells after CySC ablation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: EGFR signaling is important for the transdifferentiation of hub cells into CySCs after ablation.
source: These data are consistent with the hypothesis that EGFR signaling is important for the transdifferentiation of hub cells into CySCs after ablation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing reduced recovery in Egfr-/+ flies (Figure 4, Table 5).

claim: EGFR signaling is important for ectopic niche formation in testes recovering from genetic ablation of CySCs.
source: We conclude that EGFR signaling is important not only for recovery of CySCs but also for ectopic niche formation in testes recovering from genetic ablation of CySCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing reduced ectopic niche formation in Egfr-/+ flies (Table 6).

claim: Activation of EGFR signaling alone is not sufficient to promote the formation of ectopic niches.
source: Therefore, although EGFR signaling is important for ectopic niche formation after genetic ablation of CySCs, activation of EGFR signaling by itself is not sufficient to promote the formation of ectopic niches.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on negative experimental results.

claim: Activation of the EGFR signaling pathway in the hub is sufficient to drive hub cell proliferation and conversion to cyst lineage cells in adult testes.
source: Here, we show that activation of the EGFR signaling pathway in the hub is sufficient to drive hub cell proliferation and conversion to cyst lineage cells in adult testes.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the study.

claim: The EGFR pathway must be actively inhibited in adult hub cells to maintain their quiescence and fate.
source: Moreover, this pathway must be actively inhibited in adult hub cells to maintain their quiescence and fate, since loss of the pathway inhibitors Sprouty, Argos, or PTEN is sufficient to drive these phenotypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing that loss of inhibitors causes hub cell proliferation and transdifferentiation.

claim: The EGFR pathway is activated in hub cells upon genetic ablation of CySCs.
source: We also show that the EGFR pathway is activated in hub cells upon genetic ablation of CySCs and is important for recovery of CySCs from hub cells after ablation.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the study.

claim: The EGFR pathway is important for recovery of CySCs from hub cells after ablation.
source: We also show that the EGFR pathway is activated in hub cells upon genetic ablation of CySCs and is important for recovery of CySCs from hub cells after ablation.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the study.

claim: Signaling pathways other than EGFR could also be involved in driving hub cells out of quiescence after CySC ablation.
source: Signaling pathways other than EGFR could also be involved in driving hub cells out of quiescence after CySC ablation.
evidence: This is speculation about additional mechanisms that may be involved.

claim: In adult testes, the EGF ligand Spitz is known to be secreted from germ cells and received by cyst cells.
source: In adult testes, the EGF ligand Spitz is known to be secreted from germ cells and received by cyst cells, where activation of the EGFR pathway is essential for their proper encystment of the germ cells (Sarkar et al., 2007; Schulz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of cyst lineage cells, EGF ligands are still secreted from the germ cells but are received by the hub cells instead, promoting their conversion to new CySCs.
source: In the absence of cyst lineage cells – for example, after genetic ablation of CySCs and early cyst cells – we propose that EGF ligands are still secreted from the germ cells but are received by the hub cells instead, promoting their conversion to new CySCs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: After genetic ablation of all CySCs and early cyst lineage cells, testes rarely recover CySCs in the absence of germ cells.
source: In support of this model, after genetic ablation of all CySCs and early cyst lineage cells, testes rarely recover CySCs in the absence of germ cells (Figure 4; Table 5; Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and prior research.

claim: Hub cells do not divide and convert to CySCs after genetic ablation of only some, but not all, CySCs and early cyst lineage cells.
source: Furthermore, hub cells do not divide and convert to CySCs after genetic ablation of only some, but not all, CySCs and early cyst lineage cells (Hétié et al., 2014), consistent with the idea that hub cell quiescence is maintained by signals from cyst lineage cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Hub cell quiescence is maintained by signals from cyst lineage cells.
source: Furthermore, hub cells do not divide and convert to CySCs after genetic ablation of only some, but not all, CySCs and early cyst lineage cells (Hétié et al., 2014), consistent with the idea that hub cell quiescence is maintained by signals from cyst lineage cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: After CySC ablation, hub cell proliferation and conversion to CySCs are driven by EGFR signaling, promoted by a new signal (EGF ligands from germ cells) not normally received by the hub, and by loss of an existing signal (the EGFR inhibitor Argos from cyst lineage cells).
source: We propose a model (Figure 5) where, after CySC ablation, hub cell proliferation and conversion to CySCs are driven by EGFR signaling, promoted by a new signal (EGF ligands from germ cells) not normally received by the hub, and by loss of an existing signal (the EGFR inhibitor Argos from cyst lineage cells).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Once CySCs recover, the inhibitory signal returns, causing EGFR signaling levels in the hub to diminish.
source: Once CySCs recover, the inhibitory signal returns, causing EGFR signaling levels in the hub to diminish.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on inference from experimental findings.

claim: Recovery from genetically-induced tissue damage depends on the coordination of signals between different cell types within the testis stem cell niche.
source: Recovery from genetically-induced tissue damage thus depends on the coordination of signals between different cell types within the testis stem cell niche.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: In the Drosophila ovary, escort cells can convert into new FSCs under starvation conditions or upon forced activation of mTOR or Toll signaling.
source: A similar example of cellular plasticity in a stem cell niche was recently described in the Drosophila ovary, where two types of stem cells, germline stem cells and somatic follicle stem cells (FSCs), are housed in distinct niches at the apical ends of each ovary. A niche for FSCs is created by adjacent escort cells (aka inner germarial sheath cells), which do not give rise to new FSCs under normal conditions; however, under starvation conditions or upon forced activation of mTOR or Toll signaling in escort cells, these cells can convert into new FSCs (Rust et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the mouse small intestine, quiescent Paneth cells can replace stem cells that are lost as a result of inflammation-induced damage or irradiation to the tissue.
source: Another example comes from the mouse small intestine, where quiescent Paneth cells, which create a niche for adjacent Lgr5+ stem cells, can replace stem cells that are lost as a result of inflammation-induced damage or irradiation to the tissue (Schmitt et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ability of quiescent niche cells to convert to stem cells in response to tissue damage is likely to be a general feature of adult stem cell niches.
source: The ability of quiescent niche cells to convert to stem cells in response to tissue damage is therefore likely to be a general feature of adult stem cell niches.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple examples from different organisms.

claim: In flies recovering from genetic ablation of CySCs, when Egfr gene dosage is reduced, transdifferentiation of hub cells into CySCs happens less often than in control flies.
source: In flies recovering from genetic ablation of CySCs, when Egfr gene dosage is reduced, transdifferentiation of hub cells into CySCs and ectopic niche formation are both affected, happening less often than in control flies (Figure 4; Table 5; Table 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: In flies recovering from genetic ablation of CySCs, when Egfr gene dosage is reduced, ectopic niche formation happens less often than in control flies.
source: In flies recovering from genetic ablation of CySCs, when Egfr gene dosage is reduced, transdifferentiation of hub cells into CySCs and ectopic niche formation are both affected, happening less often than in control flies (Figure 4; Table 5; Table 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: In otherwise wild-type flies, forced activation of EGFR signaling in hub cells is sufficient for hub cell transdifferentiation but not for ectopic niche formation.
source: However, in otherwise wild-type flies, forced activation of EGFR signaling in hub cells is sufficient for hub cell transdifferentiation (Table 2) but not for ectopic niche formation.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data.

claim: Hub cell transdifferentiation and ectopic niche formation are both common in testes with forced expression of cell cycle activators or knockdown of a cell cycle inhibitor in hub cells.
source: This result is surprising because hub cell transdifferentiation and ectopic niche formation are both common in testes with forced expression of cell cycle activators or knockdown of a cell cycle inhibitor in hub cells (Hétié et al., 2014; Greenspan and Matunis, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No ectopic niches were reported in testes after depletion of the transcription factor Escargot from the hub.
source: Interestingly, no ectopic niches were reported in testes after depletion of the transcription factor Escargot from the hub, which causes hub cells to transdifferentiate into CySCs without also re-entering the cell cycle, resulting in the complete loss of hub cells over time (Voog et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The transdifferentiation of hub cells to CySCs does not by itself cause ectopic niche formation.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that the transdifferentiation of hub cells to CySCs does not by itself cause ectopic niche formation, and that additional factors must come into play in some cases to push testes towards this abnormal phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Additional factors must come into play in some cases to push testes towards ectopic niche formation.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that the transdifferentiation of hub cells to CySCs does not by itself cause ectopic niche formation, and that additional factors must come into play in some cases to push testes towards this abnormal phenotype.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental observations.

claim: PH3-positive cells were detected in 29–32% of positive control testes with Rbf knockdown in the hub.
source: As expected, PH3-positive cells were detected in 29–32% of these positive control testes (E132-Gal4, Gal80ts > UAS-Rbf-RNAi; n = 291 testes; Table 1; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the positive control.

claim: PH3-positive hub cells were not detected in negative control testes expressing GFP-RNAi.
source: Importantly, PH3-positive hub cells were not detected in testes from flies serving as negative controls (E132-Gal4, Gal80ts > UAS-GFP-RNAi; n = 237 testes; Table 1; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is experimental data from the negative control.

claim: In control testes expressing the G-TRACE cassette alone, hub cell nuclei were marked with both RFP and GFP, but cyst lineage cells outside the hub remained unmarked.
source: In control testes expressing the G-TRACE cassette alone (E132-Gal4, Gal80ts > G-TRACE), hub cell nuclei were marked with both RFP (real-time Gal4 expression) and GFP (permanent marking expression), but cyst lineage cells outside the hub remained unmarked, as expected (Table 3; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the control for lineage tracing experiments.

claim: In testes over-expressing components of the EGFR/MAPK pathway in the hub together with G-TRACE, GFP-marked nuclei were found outside the hub in significant numbers of testes.
source: In testes over-expressing components of the EGFR/MAPK pathway in the hub together with G-TRACE, hub cell nuclei were again marked with RFP and GFP, but we also found GFP-marked nuclei outside the hub in significant numbers of testes (Table 3; Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is experimental data from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Most of the GFP-marked nuclei outside the hub had little to no detectable RFP, indicating that the E132-Gal4 hub cell driver was no longer expressed in these cells.
source: Most of the GFP-marked nuclei outside the hub had little to no detectable RFP, indicating that the E132-Gal4 hub cell driver was no longer expressed in these cells.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: The morphology and arrangement of GFP-marked nuclei outside the hub suggest that these cells are cyst lineage cells that have lost their hub cell identity.
source: This observation, together with the morphology and arrangement of these nuclei, suggests that the GFP-marked cells outside the hub are cyst lineage cells that have lost their hub cell identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Sprouty is a cytoplasmic protein that is expressed in response to EGFR signaling and inhibits the pathway by a negative-feedback mechanism inside the signal-receiving cell.
source: One of these is Sprouty, a cytoplasmic protein that is expressed in response to EGFR signaling and inhibits the pathway by a negative-feedback mechanism inside the signal-receiving cell (Casci et al., 1999; Hacohen et al., 1998; Kramer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PTEN has been shown to inhibit EGFR within signal-receiving cells by promoting EGFR degradation.
source: In addition to Sprouty, Phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN), best known as an inhibitor of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway, has been shown to inhibit EGFR within signal-receiving cells, in this case by promoting EGFR degradation (Vivanco et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Argos is a secreted protein that acts extracellularly by binding to and sequestering the EGF ligand Spitz.
source: The final negative regulator of the EGFR pathway we examined, Argos, is a secreted protein that acts extracellularly by binding to and sequestering the EGF ligand Spitz (Golembo et al., 1996; Klein et al., 2004; Schweitzer et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Argos is induced by EGFR signaling.
source: However, Argos is induced by EGFR signaling (Golembo et al., 1996), which occurs at high levels in cyst lineage cells in adult testes (Chen et al., 2013; Fairchild et al., 2016; Schulz et al., 2002), suggesting that cyst lineage cells could be a source of Argos in the testis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: EGFR signaling occurs at high levels in cyst lineage cells in adult testes.
source: However, Argos is induced by EGFR signaling (Golembo et al., 1996), which occurs at high levels in cyst lineage cells in adult testes (Chen et al., 2013; Fairchild et al., 2016; Schulz et al., 2002), suggesting that cyst lineage cells could be a source of Argos in the testis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cyst lineage cells could be a source of Argos in the testis.
source: However, Argos is induced by EGFR signaling (Golembo et al., 1996), which occurs at high levels in cyst lineage cells in adult testes (Chen et al., 2013; Fairchild et al., 2016; Schulz et al., 2002), suggesting that cyst lineage cells could be a source of Argos in the testis.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge.

claim: In control testes, immunostaining for dpERK revealed consistently high pathway activation in cyst lineage cells but not in hub cells.
source: As expected based on previous studies, in control testes, immunostaining for dpERK revealed consistently high pathway activation in cyst lineage cells but not in hub cells (Figure 4A; Chen et al., 2013; Fairchild et al., 2016; Kiger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is experimental data consistent with prior research.

claim: At 2 days post-ablation, most testes have not yet recovered early cyst lineage cells.
source: As expected, dpERK staining levels appear much lower in the area adjacent to the hub in cyst lineage-ablated testes compared to controls, since most testes have not yet recovered early cyst lineage cells at 2 days post-ablation (Hétié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: At 7 days after CySC ablation, 80% of control Egfr+/+ testes had regained CySCs and early cyst cells while maintaining a hub and germ cells.
source: After 7 days of recovery, consistent with previous studies, 80% of control Egfr+/+ testes (n = 225) had regained CySCs and early cyst cells while maintaining a hub and germ cells.
evidence: This is experimental data consistent with prior studies.

claim: At 7 days after CySC ablation, testes from Egfr-/+ flies had a significantly different distribution of phenotypes, with only 45% regaining CySCs and early cyst cells while maintaining a hub and germ cells.
source: By contrast, testes from Egfr-/+ flies had a significantly different distribution of phenotypes, with only a minority of testes (45%, n = 142) regaining CySCs and early cyst cells while maintaining a hub and germ cells; most testes had only a hub or a hub and germ cells at their apex (Figure 4D; Table 5).
evidence: This is experimental data showing the effect of reduced EGFR.

claim: Fourteen days after CySC ablation, the percentage of testes that had regained CySCs and early cyst cells while maintaining a hub and germ cells remained lower in Egfr-/+ flies (55%) than in control Egfr+/+ flies (81%).
source: Fourteen days after CySC ablation, the percentage of testes that had regained CySCs and early cyst cells while maintaining a hub and germ cells remained lower in Egfr-/+ flies (55%, n = 116) than in control Egfr+/+ flies (81%, n = 151; Table 5).
evidence: This is experimental data showing sustained effect of reduced EGFR.

claim: The percentage of recovered testes with ectopic niches in Egfr-/+ flies (12%) was significantly lower than in control Egfr+/+ flies (29%).
source: The percentage of recovered testes with ectopic niches in Egfr-/+ flies (12%, n = 270) was significantly lower than in control Egfr+/+ flies (29%, n = 487, p < 0.0001; Table 6).
evidence: This is experimental data showing the effect of reduced EGFR on ectopic niche formation.

claim: Driving expression of constitutively active EGFR or Sprouty RNAi in adult hub cells for 14 days resulted in no ectopic niches.
source: We drove expression of constitutively active EGFR or Sprouty RNAi in adult hub cells (using E132-Gal4, Gal80ts) or Argos RNAi in adult cyst lineage cells (using C587-Gal4, Gal80ts), but we found no ectopic niches in any testes (n = 35, 285, or 291 testes, respectively).
evidence: This is experimental data showing negative results.

claim: Driving expression of Argos RNAi in adult cyst lineage cells for 14 days resulted in no ectopic niches.
source: We drove expression of constitutively active EGFR or Sprouty RNAi in adult hub cells (using E132-Gal4, Gal80ts) or Argos RNAi in adult cyst lineage cells (using C587-Gal4, Gal80ts), but we found no ectopic niches in any testes (n = 35, 285, or 291 testes, respectively).
evidence: This is experimental data showing negative results.

claim: Upon ligand binding, EGFR becomes active and positively regulates Ras.
source: Upon ligand binding, EGFR becomes active and positively regulates Ras; activated Ras initiates a signaling cascade that ultimately activates MAPK, which phosphorylates Pointed, the major activating transcription factor of the pathway (reviewed in Lusk et al., 2017; Shilo, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the EGFR pathway supported by citations.

claim: Activated Ras initiates a signaling cascade that ultimately activates MAPK.
source: Upon ligand binding, EGFR becomes active and positively regulates Ras; activated Ras initiates a signaling cascade that ultimately activates MAPK, which phosphorylates Pointed, the major activating transcription factor of the pathway (reviewed in Lusk et al., 2017; Shilo, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the EGFR pathway supported by citations.

claim: MAPK phosphorylates Pointed, the major activating transcription factor of the EGFR pathway.
source: Upon ligand binding, EGFR becomes active and positively regulates Ras; activated Ras initiates a signaling cascade that ultimately activates MAPK, which phosphorylates Pointed, the major activating transcription factor of the pathway (reviewed in Lusk et al., 2017; Shilo, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the EGFR pathway supported by citations.

claim: Two regulatory residues in ERK/MAPK are phosphorylated upon pathway activation and can be detected by antibodies specific for dpERK.
source: Two regulatory residues in ERK/MAPK (encoded by the rolled gene in Drosophila) are phosphorylated upon pathway activation and can be detected by antibodies specific for dpERK (Biggs et al., 1994; Gabay et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pathway activation markers supported by citations.

claim: Four EGF ligands have been identified in Drosophila: Gurken, Keren, Spitz, and Vein.
source: Four EGF ligands have been identified in Drosophila: Gurken, Keren, Spitz, and Vein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila EGF ligands.

claim: Vein is produced as a secreted protein.
source: Vein is produced as a secreted protein, but the other three are produced as inactive membrane precursors that must be cleaved to produce the active, secreted form of the ligand (reviewed in Shilo, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Gurken, Keren, and Spitz are produced as inactive membrane precursors that must be cleaved to produce the active, secreted form of the ligand.
source: Vein is produced as a secreted protein, but the other three are produced as inactive membrane precursors that must be cleaved to produce the active, secreted form of the ligand (reviewed in Shilo, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.
